title: From Purpose to Practice
author: Whitney Whealdon
summary: Whitney Whealdon closes a four-part series on reading comprehension with a concrete classroom example, teaching Gary Soto's poem Oranges under two different purposes. In a standards-based lesson the poem becomes a vehicle for figurative language, structure and theme, with close-read annotation and graphic organizers aimed at standards such as RL.7.4 and RL.7.2. In an understanding-based lesson the aim is what students learn about words, the world, and themselves and others, so the teacher begins with open reactions, checks the inferences the poem depends on, and deepens understanding through targeted rereads. She argues that the two lessons can look alike from the back of the room, yet standards-based instruction lets students show mastery without deeply comprehending the text. Standards are not discarded: a device such as symbolism is taught explicitly when it helps students express what they understand. She concludes that comprehension sits on a quality continuum and that instruction should be organised around what students can learn from a text rather than mastery of standards.
points: The same questions and close reading can serve either purpose, so what separates the two models is what counts as successful learning, not the activities themselves.
Standards contain no comprehension goal about building knowledge of words, the world and other people, which the author identifies as a structural gap in standards-based planning.
The understanding-based sequence starts with student wonderings, checks the inferences the poem depends on, and only then chooses rereads based on what students are still working out.
Teaching a standard's skill, such as symbolism, is legitimate when it serves as a tool for constructing meaning rather than as the end of the lesson.
Because comprehension is a continuum shaped by reader, text, task and context, the teacher's question shifts from whether students comprehend to how well.
quotes: Traditionally, we’ve mistaken meeting the expectations of grade-level standards and understanding the texts we read as being the same purpose.

What’s especially different about focusing on students’ ability to read, understand, and express understanding rather than aligning instruction to standards is that the understanding-based model identifies building knowledge as a core purpose. No comprehension standards specifically focus on building knowledge about words, the world, ourselves, and others, so that purpose is missing from the standards-based model.

The problem isn’t necessarily the content of the questions or whether a student is rereading a text multiple times or engaging in a “close read.” A teacher organizing instruction around standards may ask a few questions similar to questions a teacher organizing instruction around understanding might ask, or they both might engage students in close reading a text.
And this is where we make our mistake: When meeting the expectations of standards becomes our instructional goal, students can successfully demonstrate learning without deeply comprehending the text.

Note: My approach of teaching an idea from a standard is different from aligning instruction to standards because I’m teaching the knowledge and/or skill of a standard as a tool for constructing meaning. It is not the goal or end of learning.
Comprehension happens on a quality continuum. It isn't binary. The idea that we either comprehend or not is a faulty construct.

If we want students to become better at reading, understanding, and expressing their understanding of complex, grade-level texts, then we need to organize our instructional experiences around that, not mastery of standards.
